opus-5.5.text:
I think it changes the cost structure more than people initially expect, but probably not in the way the most optimistic version of the story goes.

Right now, when we collect real-robot data, the dominant cost isn't really the hardware. A robot arm, even a fairly good one, you buy once and amortize. The recurring cost is the human operator sitting there teleoperating, hour after hour. You're paying for their time, their training, and also their fatigue. After a few hours, the quality of demonstrations drops: they get slower and less consistent, and you end up filtering out a lot of what they produce. So the effective cost per *useful* trajectory is quite high.

If you can replace that operator with a model, even a decent but imperfect policy, a few things happen. First, the marginal cost of an hour of data collection drops toward the cost of electricity and wear on the robot. The model doesn't get tired, and you can run it overnight. Second, you can parallelize much more easily. One human can really only operate one setup at a time, but one policy can drive dozens of robots, with maybe one person supervising and resetting scenes.

But there are two catches I always try to emphasize.

The first is that the bottleneck shifts from *operating* to *resetting* and *supervising*. Someone still has to put the objects back, fix things when the robot knocks something off the table, and intervene when the policy gets stuck. If you don't solve autonomous resets, you've moved the human cost somewhere else rather than eliminated it.

The second, and I think more important, is the question of what the data is *for*. Data generated by a model is shaped by that model's distribution. If you just let a policy collect data and train on it, you can end up reinforcing its own habits and blind spots. Human demonstrations are expensive partly because they carry information the model doesn't have yet. So model-driven collection is most valuable when it's paired with some signal of success, like a reward, a verifier, or human correction on failures, so that you're actually learning something new and not just generating more of the same.

So my rough view: per-hour cost could drop by something like an order of magnitude, and scale becomes much less constrained by headcount. But the cost per unit of *new information* falls less dramatically, and the teams that win will be the ones that design the loop well: model does the bulk of the work, humans spend their limited time exactly where the model fails. That's where I think the real leverage is.

r001.rationale: The response says the dominant recurring cost is the human operator’s time, training, and fatigue, while robot hardware is bought once and amortized.

r002.rationale: It predicts that model-driven collection could lower the per-hour cost by roughly an order of magnitude and reduce dependence on headcount.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it would change the cost structure pretty fundamentally, but maybe not in the way people first imagine.

Right now, when you collect real-robot data, the biggest line item isn't the robot. It's the human. You need someone teleoperating, you need them trained, you need them to stay attentive for hours, and you need them to produce demonstrations that are consistent enough to learn from. That's labor cost, plus management cost, plus the hidden cost of variance across operators. So if a trained model could take over that role, the marginal cost of each additional episode drops dramatically, because you're essentially paying for electricity, wear and tear, and some supervision rather than a salary per hour of data.

But I'd be careful about saying the total cost goes to zero. A few things happen. First, you shift from paying for data collection to paying for data curation. A model operating the robot will generate a lot of trajectories, and many of them will be mediocre or outright failures. Someone, or some system, still has to filter, label success and failure, and decide what's worth keeping. Second, the model's data is only as diverse as the model's behavior. Humans naturally explore, they improvise when something goes wrong, they do things slightly differently each time. A model tends to collapse toward what it already knows. So you can end up with a lot of data that's cheap but not very informative, and you have to spend effort engineering diversity back in.

Third, there's a bootstrapping question. To have a model good enough to operate the robot, you already needed a decent amount of human data to get it there. So in practice it's not replacement, it's a flywheel. You pay the expensive human cost early, to get something that works in a narrow range, then you let the model collect in that range at low cost, then humans step in again only for the hard cases and the failures.

So my honest answer is: per-sample cost goes way down, maybe by an order of magnitude or more in mature settings. Total cost to reach a given capability drops less than that, because you're now paying in a different currency, which is quality control and coverage. And the real economic unlock isn't that data is free. It's that the cost of scaling becomes decoupled from headcount, which is what lets you talk about millions of hours instead of thousands.

r001.rationale: It identifies human teleoperation, training, attention, and management as the biggest collection costs, explicitly saying the robot is not the largest line item.

r002.rationale: It predicts that a trained model would dramatically lower the marginal cost per episode, while noting that quality control and coverage still carry costs.

astra-6.text:
I think it could substantially lower the cost, especially the recurring labor cost. Once a model can operate the robot reliably, one person could supervise several robots rather than control one robot continuously. That would make it easier to scale data collection.

But the useful measure is cost per usable trajectory. You still have to pay for the robots, maintenance, resets, and human intervention when something goes wrong. If the model fails frequently or keeps collecting very similar examples, cheaper operation doesn’t necessarily mean cheaper useful data. So I’d expect a gradual transition: models handle routine collection, while people handle difficult cases and provide demonstrations that improve the model.

r001.rationale: It mentions recurring labor as a cost, but does not identify human operators as the dominant collection cost or say that robot hardware costs have fallen.

r002.rationale: It predicts a substantial cost reduction once a trained model operates the robot, allowing one person to supervise several robots instead of continuously controlling one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could significantly reduce the cost, especially the recurring labor cost. Human operators have to spend time controlling the robot for every demonstration. If a trained model can take over some of that work, you can collect more data with less human supervision.

But the cost doesn’t disappear. You still need the robots, maintenance, and people to handle failures and check data quality. So the key is how reliably the model can operate. If it requires frequent intervention or produces a lot of unusable data, the savings may be limited. I’d look at the cost per useful demonstration, rather than just the cost per hour of robot operation.

r001.rationale: The response says operator labor is a recurring cost, but does not identify managing operators as the dominant collection cost or mention that robot hardware costs have fallen.

r002.rationale: It predicts a significant cost reduction if a trained model takes over some of the work human operators do to collect demonstrations.
